elements.note: A Roman cognomen, probably first given for red hair; used as an English given name since the 1600s.
Flavius, the family name of several emperors, is usually taken from flāvus; Wiktionary marks the link as probable.
Pompey took Magnus as a title; the name later became popular in Scandinavia and Scotland.
Superlative of magnus; a Roman cognomen famously held by the dictator Quintus Fabius Maximus.
A cognomen taken by the dictator Sulla and later borne by many early saints and popes.
Name of an early pope; Clement came into English from the Latin form Clēmēns.
A Roman cognomen; the emperor Septimius Severus is the best-known bearer.
A title given to Octavian in 27 BC; it also gave the month of August.
Borne by several early saints and popes; Victoria comes from the related word victōria 'victory'.
Lucius is related to lūx in standard accounts, but the traditional reading 'born at dawn' is not certain.
Martin is clearly from Mars; Marcus (Mark) is often traced to Mars but may instead be from an Etruscan name.
Aurelius is usually linked to aureus 'golden', but an old form Auselius points to other origins, so the link is uncertain.
A Latin given name of early saints; English candid comes from the same word.
Silvanus was also the Roman god of woods and fields.
Present participle of valeō 'to be strong, be well'.
A Roman cognomen and later the regnal name of many popes.
Borrowed into Old English as ceaster 'fort, town', usually for places with a Roman past.

examples.name: Lancaster
examples.gloss: Roman fort on the River Lune

elements.note: Came into Old English as port, meaning both 'harbour' and 'market town'.
Pontefract in Yorkshire is a rare English place-name formed directly from Latin.
Borrowed early into Old English as strǣt; in place-names it usually marks a Roman road.
Old English wīc is thought to merge vīcus with a native Germanic word, so how much Latin is in each -wick is uncertain.
Theodore is unrelated to Theodoric, which is Germanic.
The stem is andr-, as in Alexander.
Nike was also the Greek goddess of victory.
One of the commonest elements in Greek names: Themistocles, Megacles and Heracles all end in -cles.
Superlative of agathós 'good'; the source of English aristocrat.
Philip was the name of several kings of Macedon, including the father of Alexander the Great.
Leander is not from this word: its first part is leōs 'people'.
The source of English democracy.
Linked to genos 'race, kin, family'.
Used for places rather than people; Naples began as the Greek Neapolis.
The herb basil has the same source, as 'the royal plant'.
Chrysostom was a nickname for the preacher John of Constantinople.
Callimachus was a Greek poet and scholar at Alexandria.
Megacles was a name in the leading Athenian family of the Alcmaeonids.
Polycrates was a 6th-century BC ruler of Samos.
Peter is a Greek translation of Cephas, the apostle's Aramaic nickname meaning 'rock'.
Especially the victor's wreath given at games and in war.
Eirene was the Greek goddess of peace; the name was borne by an 8th-century Byzantine empress.
Related to árkhō 'to rule', the source of English monarch.
French Guillaume shows the same name with the Frankish w- turned into gu-.
The same element as Old English hrōþ, found in Hrothgar.
Same word as Old English beorht, as in Æthelberht.
Related to Latin rex and Celtic rīx 'king'.
The same root as Old English wealdan 'to rule', English wield.
Same word as Old English gār, as in Edgar.
Later spread as the suffix -ard in English and French words.
Same word as Old English æþel, as in Æthelred.
Very common in women's names, as in Clotilde and Brunhild.
Same word as Old English here, as in Hereward.
Same word as Old English sige, as in Sigeberht.
Rosamund was later reinterpreted as Latin rosa munda 'pure rose'.
The Leo- of Leopold is often mistaken for Latin leo 'lion'.
The Theo- spelling is Latinised; it is unrelated to Greek theos 'god'.
Same word as Old English hām, found in many English place-names ending -ham.
Hugh began as a short form of names starting with this element.
Same word as Old English rǣd, as in Æthelred.
In Old Norse the plural regin came to mean 'the gods'.
Matilda came to England with the Normans and was borne by William the Conqueror's queen.
The Frankish Hlūdawīg became Latin Clodovicus (Clovis) and later Louis.
Not the same as the Old English place word wīc.
Same word as Old English earn, Scots erne.
